summary:
Exo Crop helps farmers choose what to plant, and when, using 25 years of NASA data for their own field.

Every year, disasters destroy about $123 billion in crops and livestock, yet many farms still plant by calendars written for an older climate. Exo Crop lets a farmer pick any field on Earth, or one of 42 example farms in the US, Central America and China. It then reads NASA weather records, NASA satellite images, and USDA crop and soil maps for that spot.

It compares the farmer's current crop rotation with better options, and shows which ones build healthier soil without cutting income. It uses the weather forecast to pick the safest day to plant, and answers questions in plain English or Spanish, showing where each fact came from.

Our sample case is a maize farm in Honduras's Dry Corridor, where the 2018 drought destroyed 72% of the maize harvest.

Plant with the sky, not the calendar. Try it at https://exo-crop.earth/
details:
What does it do?

Exo Crop helps farmers figure out what to plant and when, using NASA data for their own field. You find your field on a 3D globe, and the site flies you down from space to that spot. From there, it reads 25 years of NASA weather and satellite records, plus USDA crop and soil maps, and tells you what's been happening on your land: when it tends to dry out, how many months the soil sits bare, and how the rain has changed.

Then it does three things. It compares what you grow now with better crop rotations, so you can see which ones build healthier soil without costing you income. It looks at the next two weeks of weather, along with 25 years of similar past seasons, to find the safest day to plant. And you can ask it questions in plain English or Spanish, and it answers using your field's data and shows where every fact came from.

Why it matters

Disasters wipe out about $123 billion in crops and livestock every year, and a lot of farmers still plant by a calendar that was set for an older climate. We started with Honduras, where the 2018 drought destroyed 72% of the maize harvest in the Dry Corridor. Those farmers don't need more data. They need someone to turn that data into a clear answer. That's what we tried to build. Our motto is "plant with the sky, not the calendar."

How we built it

The site is built with Next.js, React and TypeScript, styled with Tailwind, and hosted on Vercel at exo-crop.earth. The globe is a custom WebGL renderer. For data we pull from:

- NASA: POWER for weather and soil moisture, GIBS and MODIS for satellite imagery and plant greenness, and Blue Marble for the globe.

- USDA: the Cropland Data Layer for crop history, the SSURGO soil survey, and NASS crop prices.

- Open-Meteo: the live forecast.

The question-answering feature runs on Claude through the Anthropic API. We also used AI coding tools to help us build faster, and we made our video with Playwright and HyperFrames. It runs in any browser, including on a phone.

What makes it different

Most farm tools hand you a chart. We wanted it to feel personal, so you literally fly from orbit down to your own field. The planting advice comes from finding past seasons that looked like this one, not from a fixed calendar. And every score shows its sources, what we don't know, and what you should double-check locally.

What we thought about

Satellites see kilometers, not fence lines, so we say that on the page. Income is shown as revenue, not profit, and we always point farmers back to their local extension agent before they change anything. We added full Spanish, made the planting risk readable in words and not just colors, made it work on phones, and kept saved answers that work without internet. We also stuck to crops farmers can actually get, like velvet bean and

cereal rye, instead of suggesting things that only look good on paper.
dataRefs: NASA POWER Daily Agroclimatology (rain, temperature, root-zone soil   moisture)
NASA GIBS (MODIS Terra true color and NDVI imagery)
NASA MODIS Terra MOD13Q1 v061 NDVI
Landsat WELD true-colour imagery via NASA GIBS / Worldview
projectRefs: USDA NRCS SSURGO soil survey (Soil Data Access)
USDA NASS Quick Stats (crop prices and yields)
USDA Usual Planting and Harvesting Dates (Handbook 628)
FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56 (crop water use)
FAO Rice Conference proceedings (rice water needs)
FAO: The Impact of Disasters on Agriculture and Food Security (2023)
Anthropic Claude API (AI answers in Ask Exo Crop)
